newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FULL TEXT-Murdoch's News AGM address.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FULL TEXT-Murdoch's News AGM address.

text.p: The following is a full text of an address by Rupert Murdoch, The News Corporation Ltd's chairman and chief executive, to the annual general meeting in Adelaide on Tuesday.
I would like to provide a review of the Company's operations.

No doubt, you have read our annual report, so you know the extent and size of News Corporation, especially if you also consider the operations of our associate companies in which we have very significant shareholdings, such as Independent Newspapers in New Zealand or BSkyB in the United Kingdom and myriad other important associate companies.

The year has opened in a promising way. I am on record as saying that we expect a 20 percent increase in profit for the year. We still expect that and are still aiming for that during the coming year. However, I should say that the first quarter may not be quite up to those expectations, but we will certainly be striving to make up any shortfall.
Going through our operations, let me begin with Britain, where all divisions are doing extremely well.

"The Sunday Times" has never been better. Circulation is climbing with very little promotion behind it. "The Sunday Times" is being aggressively driven and is at an all-time record in terms of circulation. It gives great leadership and it is a paper we can be proud of. "The Sun" is still selling over 4 million copies per day. "The News of the World" is selling between 4.5 million and 5 million more than its two competitors put together.

Advertising in the United Kingdom is, relatively speaking, booming. I am happy to report that last year's extreme shortages of newsprint, which were accompanied by extreme price increases, have receded, and prices of newsprint are easing, and that is showing up in our bottom line.
We expect a very good year from our newspaper division in Britain, which is one of the biggest newspaper organisations, I think, in the world.
We are very proud of what we have achieved. We have three wonderful plants in London, Liverpool and Glasgow, all of which are running very smoothly under great leadership.

BSkyB, which you all know about, is booming. Its profits are continuing to climb, and its activities are becoming not only more aggressive, but also extending in all directions. Within the next 12 months we are planning the switchover from analogue broadcasting to digital broadcasting, allowing an increase from 28 channels of television to over 150 channels, all of much greater quality and definition. Furthermore, we believe the service will be capable of home banking transactions and various other interactive services. It is the first system in the world that will do that.

We are also very proud to be able to say that we have finally negotiated the half share we are entitled to under German law of a German satellite pay television platform. That service is only just begining - and I am sure it will not take the pain or the losses or the problems that we had at BSkyB.

It will see very heavy competition and may take two or three years to come to fruition. We believe Germany, with 100 million German speaking people, represents one of the greatest markets in the world.

Our little investment in BSkyB, which grew a little out of control at one stage and frightened a lot of people, has made a lot of money and the current value of the investment is over US$7 billion. This value is not reflected in our accounts. We are very pleased with that and hope we can repeat it elsewhere.

With regard to BSkyB's profit this year, it will be up again. We will change over to digital transmission, which will have some costs associated with it. We will go there, we think, to new heights and much greater penetration and acceptance by the public.

Turning now to the United States, "TV Guide" had record profits and the free standing insert business is also doing well. That is not so much because of a great increase in business but, rather, there have been great benefits from the fall in paper prices.

At our book business, we sold ScottForseman, which we found to be of limited potential. We thought it was better to focus our efforts where our children's books and religious books are doing well. The general adult trade business has been doing badly - but that is not unique to us. The American Book Sellers' Association estimated last summer, the Northern Summer, that there were 47 percent fewer books sold than the year before.

In television, Fox Television revenues look very good both at the owned and operated stations and the network. We had a slow start to the season because of the Olympics. The Games disrupted everything for everyone accept the owners of the rights of the Olympics.

In October, Fox has been very much involved -- or will be involved next week -- in the finals of the World Baseball Series, for which we expect to get great ratings. We have great hopes for our new dramas, and we have also a new leadership in the programming departments, and expect great things of Fox in the coming year.

All seems to be going well in our takeover at New World and the 10 television stations that come with that. We expect that deal to close sometime in January or early February 1997. We will then have the added earnings from those stations.

At Twentieth Century Fox, we have the best lineup of pictures for the rest of this fiscal year than we have ever had before. That does not mean very much. Other people also have good lineups and we will have to see how the public likes ours.
However, we are feeling very confident that we are now on top of the problems at Twentieth Century Fox and that only good things lie ahead.

Finally, I am afraid that in Australia the newspapers, which I think are now all looking very good, are nonetheless suffering from the general malaise in advertising. But we are certainly holding our share of the market. Our competitors are feeling the same cold winds as the Australian economy remains somewhat in the doldrums. So, I think the best we can hope for in Australian newspapers this year will be results which are flatter than last year.

So much for the current year, and the current quarter and where we are at the moment. I would like to portray the bigger picture as to how we see things. We are now the most global media company in the world and I think probably the most vertically integrated. We believe we have suffered very often from not being able to start or do things in television. Just as we did with newspapers in the old days, we are putting tremendous effort into setting up distribution platforms everywhere we think there is a good market.
In the long term, we aspire to be one of the best, if not the best, software providers in the world. By "software" I mean news, entertainment and sport - in short, content.
In the United States, which is the largest market in the world, we are now a major free to air broadcasters and we think that is a very good position to be in.
Elsewhere, particularly where there is high disposable income in the population, we either have established or are establishing pay television platforms.

In America, we have American Sky Broadcasting, with MCI at the moment, and the venture may include other telephone companies in due course. Together we will be launching American Sky Broadcasting with over 200 channels of television by late next year. If all goes according to plan, we will be in full launch mode this time next year.

We have very great hopes for that. There are competitors who are now growing very quickly. We are not frightened of them. We think the compeititon is not the other one or two satellite providers but the whole cable industry. We are setting out to take a piece of that.

We think the prospects are very good, but time will tell and it will not be a cheap undertaking, because we have had to buy both the sprectrum from the U.S. Goverment and buy our own satellites. However, we expect them to all come together and we will launch across the entire United States at this time next year.

In South America, we have formed associations with the leading broadcasters in Mexico and in Brazil - the two biggest economies there. We have started already - we have launched in Brazil Sky Entertaintment Services.

At this stage, I believe there are only 30 or 35 channels, and these will grow to 75 channels very quickly. We think that is a great market. It is a very small investment for us, in cash terms, but we will have, I think, 36 percent of that Brazillian Investment.

In Japan, which is a superb market, there is very little cable television there. We think it is waiting for a well marketed pay television service. We are not the only ones starting there but we believe we will be the strongest. We have a great partner there in Softbank, which is the largest computer software company in Japan, and we expect that will be starting with 12 channels some time next year. Then we will migrate to a new satellite in early 1998 and have 200 channels, pay-per-view, and movies on demand.

Of course, when one enters other countries, one cannot rely on American programmes. One has to have local partners, local programming, local software in every sense of the word, as we have done in STAR. Now all our STAR channels on our AsiaSat 1 "northern beam" are in mandarin and attract extremely good audiences. On the AsiaSat 1 "southern beam" we are concentrating very much on Hindi programming for India.

When we eventually go DTH, direct-to-home, and launch digital into India, well, of course, there are other languages spoken there as well. With digital services we will then be able to cater for them.

One development which is very pleasing is our sports programming in India, which was beginning to get very expensive. We have now formed a partnership with our former sports programming competitor, ESPN of the United States. We will maintain an ESPN channel and a STAR Sports channel.

We have the long term rights in most countries to major sporting events and we will be doing in Asia what we intend to do elsewhere in the world, that is, use sports as a "battering ram" and a lead offering in all our pay television operations.

I should just warn you that this all sounds very exciting - and it is very exciting - but we are on the cutting edge of new technology. Luckily, we own some of that technology. Our company, News Digital Systems, which is based half in Britain and half in Israel, is doing very well. It not only manufactures the "smart cards" and the encryption technology but also the actual digital compression technology. We will be floating that company in the next two or three weeks as a separate company selling about 20 percent of it in order to make it more dependent and to reassure our competitors and third parties with whom we do business.

These technological changes are coming and we think it is a wonderful thing that we are contemplating; that is, a marriage of digital technology with computers and television. We think that will give satellite a very important window in distribution of television for the next 10 or 20 years when it comes to countries like America or Europe.
When it comes to the developing world, it is probably a 50 year window. However, what can be achieved now with satellites and what will be achieved in another five or 10 years is truly amazing.

We do have the technology and the people who understand it. We also have the experience, begun at BskyB, in servicing the public, bringing them events, selling these programmes, and doing so profitably.

As I said at the beginning of this presentation, more important than our distribution plans (which we think can be very profitable) is providing the content that goes out -- whether it be made in Britain, Australia, the United States, China, India or wherever.

In the long term, we have to channel the profits that we make from distribution into building tremendous franchises. Televised news, I would say, in all its forms: general and specialised; data, in its various media, from newspapers through the Internet and through to television. That is why the launching last week of our own news channel, Fox News, was so important. To start with, that channel will be simply an American 24-hour news channel, and already it has been acclaimed by the critics.
We expect to have that channel available here within a few months on FOXTEL, and people will be able to see it here and all around the world. Just as they do with CNN.

With regard to entertainment, we have to keep attracting more talented people everywhere around the world - to make film, to make television, in all its forms, and to build franchises. We have formed, for instance, a partnership in America with one of the leading producers of children's programming and we expect to have a world-wide children's channel. The material on those channels, the language, and the actual shows will vary country by country. We think that there is a tremendous opening for children's television and we will be devoting significant resources to that initiative.

Sport absolutely overpowers film and everything else in the entertainment game. You have heard what we have been doing with Super League in Australia. There has been an unfortunate holdup, but it is going to be a wonderful asset to have now that we are free to get the competition under way.

Football, of all sports, is number one. Look at what we have done in Britain with our Premier League soccer, and now with the Rugby Union and Rugnby League in the United Kingdom as well. We expect the next three World Cups will have a significant place on our platforms. Sport will remain very important and we will be investing in and acquiring the long-term rights.
I think that sums up where we are. We have not taken our eyes off the business of building long-term assets, which we think are with content and franchises.

Finally, we have now taken our eyes off making profits, either. We know that we have to be not only viable and profitable but also that we should stay strong and liquid. You might have read last Friday that we were offered and accepted US$1 billion worth of long-term notes; their maturations are spread over four tranches - 12 years, 20 years, 40 years, and 100 years - at an average interest rate of about eight percent.
We now have US$2.5 billion in the bank and we intend to leave it there.

We have outlined all these plans to show you where we are and what we plan to go. As far as possible, we will finance them out of current cash flow to maintain liquidity so that we will be ready to take new opportunities as they arise.
Thank you very much for being here today.
It is always a great pleasure to be back in Adelaide and to be with so many friends and familiar shareholders. I can assure you that all of us in the company are working very hard for you.
Thank you.
